EXTRA CLASS · DINOSAURS · 33 CARDS · AGES 3–5

The Dinosaurs class — every card carries its own move.

Thirty-three dinosaurs, thirty-three ways to move: stomp like a T. rex, make three pretend horns, stretch your neck up high, flap and glide. Every card prints one activity under its name, every dinosaur has its lesson and printable twin right here — and the deck opens with the six dinosaurs everybody asks for first.

Meet the dinosaurs ↓The printable set ↗
HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Read the card. Do the move. Then go deeper.

Every card in this deck does two jobs: it names one dinosaur and it prints one activity — an “Activity:” line the card means literally. The short pages on this shelf show each card, quote its action word for word, and add one way to make the move into tonight’s game. When one dinosaur becomes a favorite, its lesson page carries the full teaching — what the name means, the facts a grown-up tells, the parent script, the questions to ask — and the library page holds the printable twin with a download button.

The deck opens with the six every child asks for first — the famous red hunter, the three-horned one, the plated one, the tall one, the flyer and the quick one — and then walks the rest of the prehistoric world in file order: armored tanks, trumpet-heads, sail-backs, four-winged gliders and the sea king. For the wild side beyond the Cretaceous, the Animals & Their Habitats class and the Animal Categories class sort today’s animals the same way this deck sorts the ancient ones.

ALL THIRTY-THREE DINOSAURS

Meet the deck — six favorites first.

Every card in the owner’s order: Tyrannosaurus Rex, Triceratops, Stegosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Pterodactyl and Velociraptor lead the way, then the rest of the prehistoric world. Read every card right here on this page.

WHERE THIS CLASS FITS

Beside the habitat class and the animal families.

Dinosaurs sit at one end of the animal story. The Animals & Their Habitats class walks where animals live today — meadow to ocean to ice — and the Animal Categories class sorts every animal family from pets to primates. This deck adds the ancient cast: who the hunters and plant eaters were, and how a body built for one job can become tonight’s game. For more move-like-an-animal play after the deck is done, the Animal Walks rules page on the school’s games shelf turns the same idea into a party game.

Dino moves are real learning. Every stomp, swish and glide on these cards is a body skill in disguise — do the move first, name the facts second, and let the favorite dinosaur pick the order.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tyrannosaurus Rex — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Tyrannosaurus Rex through its action — the stomp — so the most famous dinosaur arrives as something to do, not just a picture to name.

What is this?

Tyrannosaurus Rex was a giant meat eater that walked on two strong legs, with a head the size of a fridge and arms smaller than yours.

What does it mean?

Meeting the T. rex through movement teaches size by feel: a giant footstep, a giant pause, a giant sound — scale is something the body learns before the ruler shows it.

What does the child need to know?

Just floor space and brave feet. Optional: a drum, a pot, or your own hands for the giant footstep sound.

Why this matters

Every child meets the T. rex eventually — this card makes that meeting active. The stomp is honest too: the real animal shook the ground its own way.

What it teaches

Size comparison, big-motor control (a stomp needs balance), sound play, and the idea that teeth and arms can be different sizes on one animal.

Words to learn

Tyrannosaurus RexT. rexhunterstompteethgianttiny arms

Say this to your child

“"Here is the king of the dinosaurs — Tyrannosaurus Rex! Look how BIG its mouth opens. And look — its arms are tiny! Stand up tall like a T. rex. Lift your giant foot... and STOMP! One more stomp — I can feel the ground shaking!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and read the name slowly — Tyrannosaurus-Rex — then say its short name: T. rex.
  2. Point out the three things the picture shows: the huge open jaw, the tiny arms, the thick tail.
  3. Tell the facts: teeth as long as bananas, body as long as a school bus, arms too small to even reach its mouth.
  4. Practice the action together: stand tall, lift one foot high, and STOMP — twice.
  5. Ask what a stomp would sound like outside — then let the whole room be Cretaceous ground for two minutes.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a coral-red hunter stands with its huge jaw open wide, white teeth showing, two tiny arms in front and a thick tail behind — the exact giant the stomp belongs to.

Ask your child

"Which is bigger — its teeth or its arms?" "How many stomps does a T. rex need to cross your room?" "What does a baby T. rex stomp sound like?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may stomp everywhere for the rest of the day, invent a roar that scares the cat, or ask — every family’s question — whether the T. rex could eat the sofa.

Out in the real world

T. rex shows up on lunchboxes, library books and museum doors. A child who has stomped one can walk into any museum hall already knowing the star of the show.

Try it together

Harder stomping: stomp a slow pattern (big, big, small), or stomp-count to ten. Softer version: baby T. rex tiptoes — the same game at pillow volume for indoor evenings.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a T. rex do best?" (stomp and hunt with a giant bite) "Show me its arms." (tiny ones) "Was it a plant eater or a meat eater?" (meat)

This lesson pairs with the Tyrannosaurus Rex flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Triceratops — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Triceratops as the deck’s polite defender — horns it would rather not use, plants it eats all day, and a frill that does the talking.

What is this?

Triceratops was a plant eater the size of a small truck, with three horns on its face and a round bone frill at the back of its skull.

What does it mean?

The triceratops teaches defense without fighting: its horns and frill are for showing, not for hitting — a first lesson in standing your ground kindly.

What does the child need to know?

Room to make a slow triceratops walk, and fingers for horns. A paper plate makes a wonderful frill if you want a craft minute first.

Why this matters

Children already love this dinosaur; the lesson adds the WHY — what the horns are for, what the frill is made of — so the love attaches to real facts.

What it teaches

Counting to three on a real object, gentle-body control, and the plant-eater/hunter distinction that sorts the whole deck.

Words to learn

Triceratopshornfrillbeakplant eaterherdshield

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Triceratops — count its horns with me: one... two... three! It ate plants with its sharp beak, and its big frill was a shield made of bone. Put your horns on! Walk slowly like the herd. Horns are for showing — not for bumping!"”

Step by step

  1. Name it: TRI-ceratops — say "three-horned face" and count the horns on the card: one, two, three.
  2. Touch the frill on the picture — the big round collar. Explain it is real bone, a shield it wore all its life.
  3. Say what it ate: plants, snipped with a sharp beak, ground down with teeth like a horse’s.
  4. Practice the action: put on three pretend horns and pose — gentle head high, frill proud.
  5. Walk a slow herd circle together, horns showing, no bumping allowed.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a yellow triceratops smiles with two brow horns, one nose horn and a big scalloped frill — the three horns the counting game needs.

Ask your child

"How many horns does a triceratops have?" "What was the frill made of?" "Did it eat leaves or other dinosaurs?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may assign the horns names, refuse to take them off at dinner, or correct anyone who calls the frill a hat — bone, actually.

Out in the real world

Cows, goats and rhinos carry horns today for the same reasons: showing off, self-defense, and clearing brush. The triceratops is the giant in that family photo.

Try it together

Herd game: everyone poses as triceratops and walks a slow circle; one player is the wind and tries to make someone giggle out of pose. Harder: count horns on THREE different horned cards.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many horns?" (three) "What does it eat?" (plants) "What is the frill for?" (a shield)

This lesson pairs with the Triceratops flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Stegosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Stegosaurus through its two famous features — the back plates and the tail spikes — then turns the tail swish into the practice game.

What is this?

Stegosaurus was a plant eater with a double row of leaf-shaped plates along its spine and four long spikes at the end of its tail.

What does it mean?

The stegosaurus shows that protection can be beautiful: the plates are display and maybe temperature control, the spikes are the last-resort answer.

What does the child need to know?

Space for slow tail swings; a scarf, sock or ribbon for the tail makes the game twice as good.

Why this matters

The plates-versus-spikes pairing sets up an idea children reuse all year: some body parts say look-at-me, others say careful — and one animal can carry both.

What it teaches

Slow-body control (a good swish is slow), the near/far idea (plates far from danger, spikes at the tip), and honest paleontology — the plum-sized brain fact.

Words to learn

Stegosaurusplatesspikestailswishplant eaterdefense

Say this to your child

“"Here is the Stegosaurus! Look at the plates on its back — like rows of leaves. And four spikes on its tail! Tuck your tail in... swish it slowly... SWISH! Now freeze — plates tall, tail still. A statue stego is a safe stego."”

Step by step

  1. Name it and trace the plates on the card from head to tail — big, bigger, biggest.
  2. Say what the plates may have done: looked proud, maybe warmed and cooled the body like a radiator.
  3. Point to the tail tip: four spikes — the only fighting part, and it points AWAY from the stegosaurus.
  4. Practice the action: tuck your scarf-tail in and swish it slowly — swish, swish, whoosh.
  5. Freeze: plates up, tail still. A frozen stegosaurus is invisible to hungry hunters — that is the game.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a green stegosaurus shows a row of leaf-shaped plates down its back and a tail lifting with four spikes — the swish and the freeze in one picture.

Ask your child

"Which end has the spikes — head or tail?" "What do you think the plates were for?" "Was stegosaurus a hunter or a plant eater?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may wear the scarf-tail all afternoon, invent a swish dance, or proudly report the plum-brain fact to a grandparent — it is the best fact in the deck.

Out in the real world

Porcupines and stink badgers carry their defense the same way: visible, at the back, pointed away. The plates have a living echo in frilled lizards — display first, fight never.

Try it together

Plate math: line up plates smallest to biggest. Tail tag: the swisher may tag only with a slow-motion swish. Softer version: feather tail for indoor play.

Understanding check

Ask: "What grows on its back?" (plates) "What grows on its tail?" (four spikes) "Does the tail point toward danger or away?" (away — it swings at whatever comes behind)

This lesson pairs with the Stegosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Brachiosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Brachiosaurus through height: what it means to eat where nobody else can, and the full-body stretch that is the card’s action.

What is this?

Brachiosaurus was a long-necked plant eater whose front legs stood taller than its back legs, holding its neck up like a crane over the treetops.

What does it mean?

Reaching teaches height the honest way — on tiptoe, with the whole body — and plants the seed that different bodies reach different dinners.

What does the child need to know?

Standing room and something "high" to reach toward: a door frame, a curtain rod, a real treetop on a walk.

Why this matters

Long-neck dinosaurs are the deck’s gentle giants; brachiosaurus is their tallest member, and its reach is the reason it ate alone — no competition up there.

What it teaches

Full-body stretching, tiptoe balance, and the comparative idea: taller than a house, taller than two houses — big numbers built on small bodies.

Words to learn

Brachiosaurusneckreachtreetoptallfront legsleaves

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Brachiosaurus — the tall one! Its neck goes up, UP, up... its head is higher than a house! Stretch up tall on your tiptoes... pick the very top leaves... munch, munch. Nobody else can reach that salad!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and trace the neck from body to head — up, up, up.
  2. Say the two facts: front legs longer than back legs, head as high as a four-story building.
  3. Explain the salad: nothing else could reach the top leaves, so the brachiosaurus ate alone.
  4. Practice the action: stretch both arms straight up, rise on tiptoes, and pick the highest leaf you can.
  5. Munch it slowly — then crouch and graze low like a short dinosaur, and feel the difference.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue brachiosaurus stands with its front legs tall, neck rising straight up and a small head near the top — the reaching machine itself.

Ask your child

"Which legs are taller — front or back?" "What does it eat up there?" "Could a stegosaurus reach those leaves?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may spend the evening picking everything above shoulder height and calling it treetop salad, or measure the family by brachiosaurus rules.

Out in the real world

Giraffes are the living version of the same idea: a neck that reaches a dinner nobody else can. On your next walk, find the highest leaves and ask who could reach them.

Try it together

Reach ladder: three leaves at knee, shoulder and tiptoe height — munch one at each level. Harder: how long can you hold the tiptoe reach? Count it.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a brachiosaurus eat?" (treetop leaves) "Show me its stretch." (arms up, tiptoes) "Was it the tallest one here?" (yes)

This lesson pairs with the Brachiosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Pterodactyl — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Pterodactyl — honestly a flying reptile, not a dinosaur, which children love to know — and teaches its action: flap, then glide, then land soft.

What is this?

Pterodactyl was a flying reptile with wings of skin stretched over one enormously long finger bone, a long beak and a head crest.

What does it mean?

The pterodactyl teaches the flap-then-glide rhythm of real flight — effort, then rest — and the careful landing that every flyer needs.

What does the child need to know?

A rug-length of flying space and arms that flap. Couch arms and chair seats make perfect cliffs.

Why this matters

Every deck needs a sky, and the pterodactyl is the classic. The honest quirk (a flying reptile cousin) is exactly the kind of fact that makes a four-year-old feel like a scientist.

What it teaches

Rhythm control (flap-flap-glide), soft landings, and the body-plan idea: one finger as long as the whole wing.

Words to learn

Pterodactylwingsglidebeakcrestflyreptile

Say this to your child

“"Here is the Pterodactyl — a giant of the sky! Its wings are stretched skin, held out by one super-long finger. Flap, flap, flap... now glide! Soar over the mountains... land soft on the cliff. Ready to fly again?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and trace the wings — wide, pointed, skin not feathers.
  2. Tell the finger secret: the fourth finger stretched as long as the whole arm, and the wing hung from it.
  3. Say what it ate: fish, scooped from the water with that long beak.
  4. Practice the action: flap five times, then hold arms wide and GLIDE — and land soft on the cliff.
  5. Take off again: the best flyers always take off once more.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange pterodactyl flies with wide pointed wings, a swept-back head crest and a long beak — the flyer in mid-glide.

Ask your child

"Are its wings made of feathers or skin?" "Where does a pterodactyl land to rest?" "What does it scoop from the water?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may glide from every soft surface for days, announce every landing "on the cliff," or correct the family: pterodactyls are flying reptiles — actually.

Out in the real world

Bats carry skin wings today — the same design, much smaller. Point at a bird gliding without flapping: that glide is the pterodactyl’s best trick, still working overhead.

Try it together

Cliff hopping: fly couch to chair without touching the floor. Fish scoop: someone waves a scarf fish low over the water and the flyer snatches it mid-glide.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the glide." (arms wide, hold it) "What does a pterodactyl eat?" (fish) "Skin wings or feather wings?" (skin)

This lesson pairs with the Pterodactyl flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Velociraptor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Velociraptor with its real size — the honest fact that outranks any movie — and teaches its action: three quick steps, then freeze and look.

What is this?

Velociraptor was a small, fast, feathered hunter about the size of a turkey, running on two legs with one big folding claw on each foot.

What does it mean?

Correcting the movie picture is the lesson’s superpower: real animals are more interesting than monsters, and a small fast hunter is something a child’s own body can play.

What does the child need to know?

Room for three quick steps and a freeze. Nothing else — the raptor’s whole kit is its own body.

Why this matters

Children meet velociraptors in fiction long before they meet the facts. This card hands them the truth early: small, feathered, quick — and lets their body play it.

What it teaches

Speed control with a stop (the freeze is the skill), observation habits (the look left-look right), and fact-checking confidence.

Words to learn

Velociraptorraptorquickclawfeathershunterfreeze

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Velociraptor — the quick hunter! And here is the secret: it was only as big as a turkey, and it wore feathers! Quick feet, sharp eyes. Three fast steps... FREEZE... look around... where is everybody?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: a purple runner, claws up, mouth open.
  2. Tell the true size: about as tall as a turkey — smaller than the child is now. Wait for the surprise.
  3. Tell the feather fact: raptors wore feathers, and the foot claw folded back like a pocketknife.
  4. Practice the action: three quick steps — run, run, run — then FREEZE and look left, look right.
  5. Race it: raptor sprints across the room with three freezes on the way.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a purple velociraptor runs with its claws raised and mouth open in a grin — a runner built for the quick-step game.

Ask your child

"Was a velociraptor bigger or smaller than you?" (smaller — turkey-sized) "What covered its body?" (feathers) "Show me the freeze." (stop and look)

What your child can say or do

Your child may now prefer the real raptor to the movie one, measure turkeys at the market with new respect, or freeze mid-hallway unprompted.

Out in the real world

Hawks and falcons hunt the velociraptor way — speed, then a strike, then a look around. Watch any bird in the grass: quick, quick, freeze.

Try it together

Raptor rounds: three steps, freeze, look, three more — across the whole room. Harder: freeze on a drum beat, move when it stops. Softer: baby-raptor waddle version.

Understanding check

Ask: "Was it big like a bus or small like a turkey?" (turkey) "Feathers or scales?" (feathers) "What does quick dino steps mean?" (run, then freeze and look)

This lesson pairs with the Velociraptor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Allosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Allosaurus as the famous hunter of an earlier time — its wide jaw is the star — and teaches its action: two giant roars, one whispered.

What is this?

Allosaurus was a large meat eater that lived before T. rex, with sharp teeth, ridged brows and a jaw that could swing open unusually wide.

What does it mean?

Meeting an earlier hunter builds time sense — dinosaurs ruled in shifts — and roaring with a volume switch turns big feelings into a game with an off button.

What does the child need to know?

Room to open wide (jaws and arms) and the family’s tolerance for two big roars — the whisper round restores peace quickly.

Why this matters

The allosaurus prepares children for museums: its fossils are among the most common big dinosaurs found, and many halls put one front and center.

What it teaches

Volume control (loud, louder, tiny), breath support for big sounds, and the idea of dinosaur eras — before and after.

Words to learn

Allosaurusroarjawhunterearliervolumewhisper

Say this to your child

“"Here is the Allosaurus — the big hunter from before T. rex was even born! Look how wide its mouth opens! Take a deep breath... one giant ROAR... and another! Now... whisper roars. Tiny hunter, tiny roars!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: purple, mouth open wide, spikes down the back.
  2. Tell its time: allosaurus was the giant hunter LONG before T. rex — the king of an earlier age.
  3. Tell the jaw fact: its mouth swung open wider than most hunters — a big bite needs a big door.
  4. Practice the action: one giant roar to the window, one giant roar to the door.
  5. Now the switch: roar both roars in baby-allosaurus whisper. Loud then soft is the whole game.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a purple allosaurus stands with a wide-open mouth of white teeth, a ridge of spikes down its back and two small arms — the earlier king, mid-roar.

Ask your child

"Who was the big hunter before T. rex?" (allosaurus) "Show me the wide jaw." (hands open wide) "Can you roar in whisper?" (yes — the best round)

What your child can say or do

Your child may assign the two roars to different rooms, teach the whisper round to the dog, or line up allosaurus before T. rex in a timeline on the floor.

Out in the real world

Lions and gators announce themselves with sound before anyone sees them — a roar is a hunting announcement. Where the family lives, what are the two loudest animal voices?

Try it together

Roar scale: roar one to five, one being whisper, five being giant. The allosaurus only roars ONE and TWO — the game is stopping at two.

Understanding check

Ask: "Was allosaurus before or after T. rex?" (before) "What was special about its jaw?" (swung extra wide) "Show me a whisper roar."

This lesson pairs with the Allosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Ankylosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Ankylosaurus as the deck’s tank — armor everywhere and a club that does the talking — and teaches its action: the slow, heavy swing.

What is this?

Ankylosaurus was a wide plant eater covered in bony studs, with a heavy round club of fused bone at the end of its tail.

What does it mean?

The ankylosaurus teaches defense by armor: some animals carry their shield ON their body — and its swing is slow on purpose, which children find hilarious and then imitate.

What does the child need to know?

Room for a slow semicircle swing; a soft cushion makes a safe club for the living-room version.

Why this matters

Knights and turtles already teach armor; the ankylosaurus adds the hammer. It is also the deck’s funniest silhouette, which is why children remember it.

What it teaches

Slow-motion control (the swing must be slow), cause and effect (armor outside, soft body inside), and the curl-and-unfold game for body awareness.

Words to learn

Ankylosaurusarmorstudsclubtailswingdefense

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Ankylosaurus — a walking tank! Studs all over its back, and a big bone club on its tail. Swing it sloooowly... thud! Nobody bothers an ankylosaurus! Now curl up small under your armor — one, two, three, four, five — safe!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and trace the studs on the back — armor, row by row.
  2. Point to the tail: a heavy round club, two lumps of bone grown together like a hammer.
  3. Say the rule of the swing: slow and heavy, never fast — a real club tail swung low and slow.
  4. Practice the action: hold the cushion-club and swing one slow arc around your feet... thud.
  5. Finish with the armor ball: curl up small, tuck everything in, count to five — fully protected.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a teal ankylosaurus shows oval studs across its back and a raised tail ending in a round club — the swing and the ball in one picture.

Ask your child

"What is on the end of its tail?" (a club) "Fast swings or slow swings?" (slow) "What do we do when trouble comes?" (curl into the armor ball)

What your child can say or do

Your child may appoint a cushion as a permanent pet club, curl into armor balls at bedtime, or explain that slow is stronger — the ankylosaurus rule.

Out in the real world

Turtles carry armor outside; pangolins curl into balls; rams swing heads. The ankylosaurus is all three at dinosaur size, which is why it never needs to run.

Try it together

Club course: swing once past each chair on a slow walk. Harder: keep the swing slow while someone counts faster. Softer: the armor ball rolls gently — one tumble, then unfold.

Understanding check

Ask: "What hangs on its tail?" (a bone club) "Show me the armor ball." (curl and count) "Was it a plant eater?" (yes — all that armor for a gentle animal)

This lesson pairs with the Ankylosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Archaeopteryx — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Archaeopteryx — the fossil that proved dinosaurs and birds belong to one family — and teaches its action: the wing stretch, one wing at a time.

What is this?

Archaeopteryx was a small feathered dinosaur with wings, teeth and a long bony tail — able to flutter or glide, and famous as the first bird-cousin fossil ever found.

What does it mean?

The archaeopteryx teaches the family idea: birds did not appear from nowhere — they ARE dinosaurs, still singing this morning.

What does the child need to know?

Room to bow each wing. A feather or a leaf held on the head adds instant archaeopteryx if the family wants it.

Why this matters

Every child who meets archaeopteryx owns the best fact in paleontology: birds are living dinosaurs. It reframes every pigeon forever.

What it teaches

The half-and-half idea (teeth AND feathers on one animal), gentle side-bending in the stretch, and museum literacy — the most famous fossil there is.

Words to learn

ArchaeopteryxfeatherswingsfossilbirdglideGermany

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Archaeopteryx — half dinosaur, half bird! Teeth like a dinosaur, feathers like a bird. Stretch your wings out wiiide... bow to this side... bow to that side... flap, flap, glide! Its feathers are printed in stone, and birds are its grandchildren!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: green, feathered, wings spread, long feathered tail.
  2. Name its parts both ways: teeth like a dinosaur, feathers like a bird — one animal, both families.
  3. Tell the fossil story: in Germany, in stone, its feathers printed perfectly — 150 million years old.
  4. Practice the action: stretch both wings wide... bow one wing... bow the other... now three little flutters and a glide.
  5. End with the fact that lands: your child has just met a chicken’s great-great-many-times-grandparent.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a green archaeopteryx spreads both feathered wings wide with a long feathered tail behind and running legs below — the half-way flyer, mid-stretch.

Ask your child

"What did archaeopteryx have that birds still have?" (feathers and wings) "What dinosaur parts did it keep?" (teeth and a bony tail) "Are birds dinosaurs?" (yes — living ones)

What your child can say or do

Your child may greet the next pigeon as a dinosaur, want to see the stone-feather fossil picture a hundred times, or glide from room to room with one feather aboard.

Out in the real world

Chickens, pigeons and eagles are the living branches of the archaeopteryx family. Next egg at breakfast: you are eating a dinosaur’s answer to breakfast, too.

Try it together

Wing bows: one bow per side, then flutters, then a glide to a perch. Harder: hold the glide while counting to five. Softer: sit and do the bows with arm-wings only.

Understanding check

Ask: "Did archaeopteryx have feathers or scales?" (feathers) "Show me a one-wing bow." "What are birds today?" (living dinosaurs)

This lesson pairs with the Archaeopteryx flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Baryonyx — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Baryonyx, the deck’s patient fisherman, and teaches its action: paw in the water, three-count wait, then the scoop.

What is this?

Baryonyx was a meat-eating dinosaur with a long narrow crocodile-style snout, almost a hundred teeth, one giant thumb claw — and a diet full of fish.

What does it mean?

Fishing teaches the hardest skill in childhood: waiting. The baryonyx holds still, watches the water, and strikes once — patience, modeled by a dinosaur.

What does the child need to know?

A rug river (real or imaginary) and one hand to fish with. A blue scarf makes a fine river if the family has one.

Why this matters

Not every hunter chases — some fish. The baryonyx widens the deck’s idea of hunting, and its proof is delicious: fish scales found right in its fossil belly.

What it teaches

Stillness with a countdown, one-handed scoop control, and the standing-on-one-leg balance of a real riverbank hunter.

Words to learn

Baryonyxfishsnoutclawriverwaitscoop

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Baryonyx — the fisher dinosaur! A long snout like a crocodile, and one giant claw. Stand on the bank... dip your claw... wait... wait... SCOOP! A fish! Munch, munch. Now the other paw — fishing is patient work."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: indigo-blue, long narrow snout, mouth open.
  2. Say its name meaning: heavy claw — one giant thumb claw, almost as big as a lemon.
  3. Tell the belly fact: scientists found fish scales inside a baryonyx fossil — its last supper, printed in stone.
  4. Practice the action: stand on the riverbank (one leg), dip the claw-hand in the water, hold for three seconds... SCOOP the fish.
  5. Gobble it loudly, then fish the next spot with the other hand.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an indigo-blue baryonyx leans forward with its long narrow snout open and one big claw showing — the fisher, mid-wait.

Ask your child

"What does a baryonyx eat?" (fish) "How long do we wait before the scoop?" (three seconds) "What is on its thumb?" (a giant claw)

What your child can say or do

Your child may fish from the couch for the rest of the week, enforce the three-count on everyone, or report the belly-fossil fact with enormous pride.

Out in the real world

Herons and bears fish the baryonyx way — freeze, watch, strike once. On the next pond walk, watch a heron hold still: that is the whole lesson, live.

Try it together

Fishing rounds: three catches in a row earns a fish-jump celebration. Harder: five-second waits. Softer: catch on count one — baby baryonyx are still learning.

Understanding check

Ask: "Long snout or short snout?" (long, like a crocodile) "What is for lunch?" (fish) "Show me the wait-then-scoop."

This lesson pairs with the Baryonyx flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Carnotaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Carnotaurus — the bull of the hunters — and teaches its action: horns on, head low, three poses from fiercest to silliest.

What is this?

Carnotaurus was a meat-eating dinosaur with two horn bumps above its eyes, a short snout and arms so small they were nearly useless.

What does it mean?

Posing teaches body language: the same horns can look fierce, proud or funny — and the child controls which, which is social-emotional learning wearing a dinosaur suit.

What does the child need to know?

A mirror makes the poses twice as fun but is not required. Floor space for a head-low strut.

Why this matters

The carnotaurus is the deck’s expression lesson: faces and postures carry messages, and children practice reading them on a horned dinosaur first.

What it teaches

Expressive control (fierce, proud, silly on purpose), the head-low strut balance, and the funniest anatomy fact this side of the T. rex arms.

Words to learn

Carnotaurusbullhornsposefierceproudtiny arms

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Carnotaurus — the bull hunter! Two horns above its eyes, and arms so tiny they almost disappear! Put your horns on... lower your head... POSE! Fierce! Now proud! Now the silliest pose you have!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: orange-red, two bumps above the eyes, mouth open.
  2. Say its name meaning: meat-eating bull — it even charged like one, scientists think.
  3. Tell the arm fact: smaller than a T. rex’s arms — some scientists joke they were barely there.
  4. Practice the action: two finger-horns above the eyebrows, head low — pose one, fierce; pose two, proud; pose three, silly.
  5. Everyone copies each pose — the silliest gets the loudest roar.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange-red carnotaurus stands head-low with two horn bumps above its eyes, a bumpy back and an open mouth — ready for its three poses.

Ask your child

"How many horns — two, three or four?" (two) "Show me the fierce pose." "What is funny about its arms?" (tiny!)

What your child can say or do

Your child may pose on demand all week, discover the fierce-to-silly dial works on real moods too, or measure every family member’s arms against the carnotaurus standard.

Out in the real world

Bulls lower their heads and show horns to say back off — carnotaurus did the same. Practicing the poses also gives the family words: I feel fierce, I feel proud, I feel silly.

Try it together

Pose parade: walk the room head-low, holding one pose until someone guesses it. Harder: switch poses on a clap. Softer: mirror poses face to face.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do its horns grow?" (above its eyes) "Show me tiny arms." "Name the three poses." (fierce, proud, silly)

This lesson pairs with the Carnotaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Centrosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Centrosaurus, the herd member of the horned family, and teaches its action: a gentle horn pose for greeting the whole herd.

What is this?

Centrosaurus was a plant eater with one big nose horn, a large frill edged in short spikes, and a habit of traveling in enormous herds.

What does it mean?

Gentle posing practices the greeting ritual: horns up means hello here. It also plants the herd idea — thousands of horned friends moving as one.

What does the child need to know?

Room for a slow herd circle. Every family member present becomes the herd — even one grown-up and one child counts.

Why this matters

The centrosaurus scales up friendship: its herds numbered in the thousands, and the lesson rides that number into a calm group game.

What it teaches

Slow synchronized walking (herd circle), gentle-body control, and big numbers — a thousand is a lot of triceratops cousins.

Words to learn

Centrosaurusherdnose hornfrillspikesgentletogether

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Centrosaurus — a horned friend who travels with THOUSANDS of friends! One strong horn on its nose, spikes around its frill. Put your horn on... hold your frill up... and walk the slow herd circle. Gentle horns — hello, hello!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: lime-green, big frill with small spikes, one nose horn, cream beak.
  2. Count what you see: one nose horn — just one, different from the triceratops’ three.
  3. Tell the herd fact: they walked in herds so big that scientists think thousands crossed the land together.
  4. Practice the action: nose-horn forward, arm-frill up — a gentle pose, held tall.
  5. Walk one slow herd circle together, poses showing, nobody bumping.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a lime-green centrosaurus stands with a big frill edged in small spikes, a cream beak and one nose horn — the herd member in greeting pose.

Ask your child

"How many horns on its nose?" (one) "How many friends did it travel with?" (thousands!) "Is the pose gentle or rough?" (gentle)

What your child can say or do

Your child may appoint the family as a permanent herd, lead slow circles through the hallway, or explain that one horn is plenty — the centrosaurus rule.

Out in the real world

Herds still move today: wildebeest cross rivers by the thousand, and starlings flock in clouds. The centrosaurus is the horned member of that crowd.

Try it together

Herd switch: walk the circle, and when one player calls "wind!", everyone freezes in pose. Harder: two herds cross paths and greet — horns up, pass gently.

Understanding check

Ask: "What travels in huge herds?" (centrosaurus) "Show me the gentle pose." "What does it eat?" (plants)

This lesson pairs with the Centrosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Ceratosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Ceratosaurus, the decorated hunter, and teaches its action: tap the nose for the horn, pose, stomp three, pose again.

What is this?

Ceratosaurus was a meat-eating dinosaur with one small horn on its snout, bony ridges above each eye, a ridged back and a strong swimming tail.

What does it mean?

The ceratosaurus practices posing with purpose: a hunter’s face is a tool, and the child learns to build it — tap, pose, stomp — like a routine.

What does the child need to know?

Room to stomp and pose. Doorways, windows and couch corners become the pose stations.

Why this matters

Not every horn belongs to a plant eater — the ceratosaurus breaks the pattern children just learned with triceratops, and pattern-breaking sticks.

What it teaches

Routine memory (tap, pose, stomp, pose), balance on the stomp, and the swim-tail fact as a first foray into dinosaur swimming.

Words to learn

Ceratosaurusnose hornridgeshunterposestomptail

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Ceratosaurus — the hunter with a horn on its NOSE! Tap your nose... there it is! Make your hunter pose... stomp, stomp, stomp... and pose again. A hunter checks every corner of its territory!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: deep pink, small horn on the snout, ridged back.
  2. Find the horn: one small bump right on the nose — a hunter with jewelry.
  3. Tell the tail fact: strong and tall, it swam better than most big hunters.
  4. Practice the action: tap your nose-horn... make your proudest hunter pose... stomp three steps... pose again.
  5. Pose in three places: doorway, window, couch — a hunter surveys the whole territory.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a deep-pink ceratosaurus stands with a small nose horn, ridges along its back and an open smiling mouth — the decorated hunter, ready to pose.

Ask your child

"Where does its horn grow?" (on its nose) "What could it do better than most hunters?" (swim) "Show me a pose in a new place."

What your child can say or do

Your child may patrol the apartment in hunter poses, appoint every room a territory, or tap their nose before every dramatic announcement.

Out in the real world

Rhinos carry a nose horn today — the same real estate. And crocodiles show the swimming-hunter design the ceratosaurus used: low in the water, tail doing the work.

Try it together

Territory tour: five pose stations, one pose each. Harder: add a swim-round — low walking, tail-swaying — between stations.

Understanding check

Ask: "Nose horn or eye horns?" (nose) "Show me the tap-and-pose." "Hunter or plant eater?" (hunter)

This lesson pairs with the Ceratosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Compsognathus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Compsognathus, the deck’s smallest hunter, and teaches its action: five tiny steps, counted out loud, in any direction.

What is this?

Compsognathus was a tiny fast hunter about the size of a chicken, standing on two slim legs with a long tail for balance.

What does it mean?

Small is a fact worth loving: the littlest hunter is the one a child’s body can BE. Counting steps turns tiptoeing into a real game with numbers inside.

What does the child need to know?

Any room at all — compsognathus needs the least space in the deck. Bare feet make the tiny steps quieter and better.

Why this matters

After giants, the deck gets small — and the size range is the lesson: dinosaurs came chicken-sized AND bus-sized, and both are true.

What it teaches

Counting one to five with steps, tiptoe control, and the smallness comparison that makes big dinosaurs bigger.

Words to learn

Compsognathustinystepsquickhuntersmallcount

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Compsognathus — the littlest hunter! Smaller than your teddy bear, quick as a blink. Five tiny steps now: one... two... three... four... five! Freeze! Where to next — backward? Sideways? A tiny hunter decides!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: small, teal, standing on two slim legs.
  2. Say the size: chicken-sized — it could stand on a dinner plate. Hold out a plate to prove it.
  3. Tell the belly fact: one fossil kept a whole lizard inside — dinner, preserved 150 million years.
  4. Practice the action: five tiny tiptoe steps — count them: one, two, three, four, five.
  5. Try five backward, five sideways, five in a circle — a tiny hunter goes everywhere.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a small teal compsognathus stands on slim legs with a few spots along its back — the littlest hunter, waiting for its first five steps.

Ask your child

"Bigger or smaller than your teddy bear?" (smaller!) "How many tiny steps?" (five) "Show me tiny steps in a circle."

What your child can say or do

Your child may adopt the five-count for every hallway mission, measure pets against the plate standard, or narrate five-step journeys all afternoon.

Out in the real world

Hummingbirds and wrens are today’s tiny dinosaurs — same family, still tiny, still quick. Small was always a successful way to be a dinosaur.

Try it together

Tiny missions: five steps to touch the door, five to reach the window. Harder: count backward five to one while returning. Softer: two-step version for brand-new counters.

Understanding check

Ask: "Was compsognathus big or small?" (chicken-small) "Show me five tiny steps." "What did one fossil still have inside?" (a lizard — its dinner)

This lesson pairs with the Compsognathus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Corythosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Corythosaurus, the deck’s trumpet player, and teaches its action: one long call, answered by the herd in echo.

What is this?

Corythosaurus was a duck-billed plant eater with a hollow, half-moon crest on its head — tubes inside connected to its nose like a built-in horn.

What does it mean?

Calling and echoing is a listening game in disguise: make a sound, wait for the answer. It is turn-taking, volume control and hearing practice with a dinosaur voice.

What does the child need to know?

Voices only. Hands cupped as the crest; a hallway gives a wonderful echo for free.

Why this matters

Sound is the corythosaurus’s superpower, and children adore having a GOOD reason to make noise — then a reason to stop and listen for the answer.

What it teaches

Breath control for long calls, listening and turn-taking in the echo, and the tube idea: air through a curved tube makes music.

Words to learn

Corythosauruscresttrumpetcallechoherdhollow

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Corythosaurus — the dinosaur with a trumpet on its head! Its crest is hollow, like a horn. Cup your hands... breathe in... TOOOTO! Long and proud! Now the herd answers — everyone echo back!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: bright blue, rounded crest swept back like a half moon.
  2. Say the secret: the crest is HOLLOW — air runs through tubes inside it.
  3. Tell what it did: one deep breath, one long TOOOTO that carried across the whole valley.
  4. Practice the action: hands cupped around your mouth, one long trumpet call.
  5. The herd answers: everyone else echoes — one long call back, then two short ones.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a bright-blue corythosaurus stands with a rounded crest swept back from its head — the trumpet, worn on the face.

Ask your child

"What is inside the crest?" (hollow tubes of air) "Show me a long call." "How does the herd answer?" (an echo — long, then short, short)

What your child can say or do

Your child may assign calls to every room, answer all family questions in trumpet for one whole day, or invent short-call codes for dinner.

Out in the real world

The design still works: brass trumpets, foghorns and juicing straws all do what the crest did — carry air through a tube to make it louder. Blow across a bottle top: instant corythosaurus.

Try it together

Call codes: long call means come here, two short means look. Harder: echo with matching volume — loud calls get loud echoes. Softer: whisper calls for evening herds.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the crest do?" (works like a trumpet) "Show me the long call." "What comes back after the call?" (the herd’s echo)

This lesson pairs with the Corythosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Deinonychus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Deinonychus, the hunter that rewrote the dinosaur books, and teaches its action: quick steps, a springy jump, claws up, freeze.

What is this?

Deinonychus was a fast, feathered hunter with striped coloring, a stiff tail for balance and one huge curved claw held up on the second toe of each foot.

What does it mean?

The deinonychus teaches the full sequence skill: run, jump, freeze — three controls in one row. It also carries the deck’s best science story.

What does the child need to know?

A room-length runway and safe landing space. The jump is springy, not high — feet stay under control.

Why this matters

This is the dinosaur that made scientists rethink everything — its fossils showed dinosaurs might be active, quick and bird-like. Children get the revolution in one lesson.

What it teaches

Sequencing (run-jump-freeze), springy landings, and story memory: one claw, one fossil, one whole science shake-up.

Words to learn

Deinonychusclawsicklejumpfreezestripedpack

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Deinonychus — the terrible-claw hunter! A claw on each foot, curved like a banana. Quick feet now: run-run-run... JUMP, claws up!... freeze. Do it again — the fastest hunter in the forest is standing right here!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: purple with darker stripes, mouth open, big foot claws.
  2. Say its name meaning: terrible claw — curved like a banana, held up like a switchblade.
  3. Tell the science story: its fossils made scientists rethink dinosaurs — quick, active, feathered, bird-like.
  4. Practice the action: six quick steps... JUMP with both claw-hands up... freeze like a statue.
  5. Chain it: run-jump-freeze across the whole room, one chain after another.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a purple deinonychus with darker stripes stands with its mouth open and one big sickle claw visible — the claw that changed the books.

Ask your child

"What shape is the big claw?" (curved like a banana) "Show me run-jump-freeze." "Did it hunt alone or with friends?" (with friends — in packs)

What your child can say or do

Your child may spring-jump from couch to rug with claws up, teach the freeze to friends, or demand the story of the fossil that changed everything — twice nightly.

Out in the real world

Hawks strike with talons; cats keep claws folded until needed. The deinonychus’s folding claw works like a cat’s — hidden between hunts, deadly when out.

Try it together

Claw chains: three run-jump-freezes in a row without wobbling. Harder: freeze in different shapes each time. Softer: step-jump-step for early jumpers.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is on its second toe?" (a big curved claw) "Show me the freeze with claws up." "Was it quick or slow?" (quick)

This lesson pairs with the Deinonychus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Diplodocus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Diplodocus, the deck’s bridge, and teaches its action: one arm up as the neck, one arm trailing as the tail, walking the room-long loop.

What is this?

Diplodocus was a giant plant eater as long as two cars, with most of that length in its neck and whip-thin tail, walking on four sturdy legs.

What does it mean?

Becoming a bridge — neck arm and tail arm at once — is real coordination work: two arms doing two different jobs while the feet walk.

What does the child need to know?

A long room or hallway makes the loop grand. Nothing else needed; the arms are the dinosaur.

Why this matters

The diplodocus is the deck’s pure size wonder — nothing on it bites or spikes. Its whole defense is being enormous, which is its own kind of lesson.

What it teaches

Two-arm coordination (up-arm and back-arm disagree on purpose), slow walking control, and the whip-tail science fact.

Words to learn

Diplodocusnecktailwhiplongbridgeplant eater

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Diplodocus — the long one! Neck out this way, tail out that way — as long as two cars! Walk your slow loop... neck arm munching leaves... tail arm swishing behind. Now swap — the long neck goes on the other side!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: blue, neck forward, tail back, four legs under a long body.
  2. Say the length: two cars parked end to end — and MOST of it is neck and tail.
  3. Tell the whip fact: the tail was thin like a whip, and it may have cracked it — loudest sound in the valley.
  4. Practice the action: one arm stretches up-forward as the neck, the other trails low behind as the tail. Walk a slow loop.
  5. Swap arms: now the other arm is the neck. A long dinosaur trains both ends.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue diplodocus stretches its neck forward and its whip tail back over four sturdy legs — the bridge, ready to walk.

Ask your child

"Which ends are long?" (neck and tail) "Show me the neck arm and the tail arm." "What sound might the tail make?" (a whip crack!)

What your child can say or do

Your child may walk whole days as a bridge-dinosaur, whip-crack an imaginary tail, or explain that being big was the diplodocus’s whole plan.

Out in the real world

Whiptail lizards and iguanas carry real tails for balance and signaling. The diplodocus’s whip is the record-holder — some scientists think the crack broke the sound barrier.

Try it together

Long-loop: walk the hallway as the bridge dinosaur without dropping either arm. Harder: neck arm drinks from an imaginary treetop mid-walk. Softer: arms only, sitting down.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the two long parts?" (neck and tail) "Show me the walking loop." "Meat eater or plant eater?" (plant eater — all that length just for reaching)

This lesson pairs with the Diplodocus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Euoplocephalus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Euoplocephalus, the deck’s safest dinosaur, and teaches its action: curl in, count to five tucked, unfold giant.

What is this?

Euoplocephalus was a wide plant eater with bony studs across its back, armor plates even over its eyes, and a low-swinging club tail.

What does it mean?

Curling small and unfolding big is a regulation game in disguise — the tuck is calm-down practice, the unfold is a giggle. Armor outside, soft inside.

What does the child need to know?

Floor space to curl on. A soft rug makes the best armor ball zone.

Why this matters

The eyelid armor is the fact nobody forgets — shutters that could slide over its eyes. And the curl game doubles as the deck’s quiet-time tool.

What it teaches

Body tucking (curl is a real motor skill), counting while still, and the unfold that practices big shapes after small ones.

Words to learn

Euoplocephalusarmorstudseyelidscurlclubsafe

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Euoplocephalus — the safest dinosaur! Studs on its back, armor on its eyelids, a club on its tail. Curl up small now... tuck in... count with me: one, two, three, four, five... UNFOLD! A giant armored dinosaur!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: green, wide studded back, low club tail.
  2. Find the best fact: even its EYELIDS had armor — little sliding bones like shutters.
  3. Say the plan: when trouble came, it tucked in low — armor outside, soft inside, nothing to bite.
  4. Practice the action: curl up small on the floor, arms tucked, and count to five.
  5. Unfold into a giant armored dinosaur — stand wide, stomp twice, roar once.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a green euoplocephalus shows a wide studded back and a low tail with its club — the curl-up expert, armored everywhere.

Ask your child

"Where is the weirdest armor?" (the eyelids!) "Show me the curl and the count." "What hangs low on its tail?" (the club)

What your child can say or do

Your child may curl-count at bedtime unprompted — the calm-down tool arrives for free — or slide fingers over their own eyelids explaining shutters.

Out in the real world

Armadillos and hedgehogs curl the euoplocephalus way: shield outside, soft inside. Clams and pill bugs do it too — the tuck is one of nature’s oldest tricks.

Try it together

Armor rounds: curl, count to five, unfold, stomp twice — three rounds. Harder: count to ten tucked with eyes closed. Softer: curl for three, for brand-new counters.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does it do when trouble comes?" (curls up small) "Count the tuck." (five) "Club tail or spike tail?" (club)

This lesson pairs with the Euoplocephalus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Giganotosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Giganotosaurus, the giant of the south, and teaches its action: three giant steps, then measuring how far the giant got.

What is this?

Giganotosaurus was one of the longest meat-eating dinosaurs ever found — maybe even longer than T. rex — with hand-sized teeth and a huge head.

What does it mean?

Measuring by body steps is real math: estimate, step, count, compare. The giganotosaurus makes measurement a giant-sized event.

What does the child need to know?

A hallway or room-length runway and feet for stepping. A heel-toe walk makes the steps honestly giant.

Why this matters

The T. rex question is inevitable — who wins? The honest answer (different times, different places, both enormous) teaches that big comes in more than one flavor.

What it teaches

Estimating then measuring, heel-toe walking, and the bigger-vs-longer distinction: giganotosaurus was LONGER, T. rex maybe stronger.

Words to learn

Giganotosaurusgiantstepsmeasurelongerteethsouth

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Giganotosaurus — the giant of the south! Maybe even longer than T. rex! Teeth as long as your hand! Three GIANT steps now: one... two... three! How far did the giant get? Guess — then let us measure!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: bright blue, huge head, thick tail.
  2. Say its name meaning: giant southern lizard — it lived far south, in what is now Argentina.
  3. Tell the teeth fact: as long as your hand — every single tooth.
  4. Practice the action: three GIANT steps, heel to toe, the longest steps your legs can make.
  5. Measure: how many giant steps cross the hallway? Guess first, then step it.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a bright-blue giganotosaurus stands with a huge head, open mouth of teeth and a thick tail — the southern giant, ready to step.

Ask your child

"Which was longer — giganotosaurus or T. rex?" (giganotosaurus, scientists think) "How long were its teeth?" (as long as your hand) "Show me your three giant steps."

What your child can say or do

Your child may measure every hallway in the house by giant steps, argue the T. rex rematch fairly, or hold a ruler to their hand announcing: giga tooth.

Out in the real world

Blue whales today dwarf every dinosaur — the size record is still moving. Measuring rooms by steps is how surveyors started: estimate, step, count.

Try it together

Step charts: giant, medium, tiny — three step sizes, three measurements. Harder: estimate before every measure, then check. Softer: two steps for new counters.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where did it live — north or south?" (south, in Argentina) "Show me three giant steps." "Meat eater or plant eater?" (meat — with hand-long teeth)

This lesson pairs with the Giganotosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hadrosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Hadrosaurus, the famous duck bill, and teaches its action: nibble at three heights — grass, bush and tiptoe — each with its own sound.

What is this?

Hadrosaurus was a plant eater with a wide flat duck-style beak, strong back legs and arms it could lean on — a runner and a wader both.

What does it mean?

Nibbling at three heights is a sorting game inside a movement game: the same mouth, three different dinners, three different sounds.

What does the child need to know?

Room to reach low, middle and high. A real plant to nibble NEAR (never eat) makes the lesson vivid — a houseplant counts.

Why this matters

Hadrosaurus is the deck’s history card: the first nearly complete skeleton found in North America, in 1858. Every museum’s duck-bill hall starts here.

What it teaches

Reaching to three heights (low, middle, high), sound play for each bite, and the fossil-first story: one skeleton started a whole country’s dinosaur science.

Words to learn

Hadrosaurusduck billnibbleplantsheightsfossilfirst

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Hadrosaurus — the duck-billed plant eater! Small bites, always polite. Nibble the grass — nib, nib, nib... nibble the bush — munch, munch... reach up high — CHOMP! Now the happiest dinosaur sigh: ahhhh."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: orange, duck-billed head, standing on two strong legs.
  2. Say the beak fact: wide and flat like a duck’s — it cropped plants in small polite bites.
  3. Tell the history fact: found in 1858 — the first big dinosaur skeleton dug up in North America.
  4. Practice the action: nibble low (grass sound: nib-nib-nib), middle (bush sound: munch-munch), high on tiptoe (one big CHOMP).
  5. Finish with the satisfied dinosaur sigh — the happiest plant eater in the deck.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange hadrosaurus stands tall on its back legs with a wide flat beak and a gentle eye — the famous duck bill, ready to nibble.

Ask your child

"What shape is its beak?" (flat like a duck’s) "Show me nibbling at three heights." "Big bites or small bites?" (small — always polite)

What your child can say or do

Your child may narrate all future meals in nibble-sounds, inspect every duck at the pond for family resemblance, or report the 1858 fact at show-and-tell.

Out in the real world

Ducks still strain food with the same beak plan, and horses chew side to side like duck bills did. The nibble is a living habit — breakfast proves it.

Try it together

Nibble relay: three bites at three heights, then run to the far wall and back. Harder: add a fourth height — jump-nibble. Softer: sit and nibble at two heights.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is special about its mouth?" (a wide duck bill) "Show me the high nibble." "Was it a hunter or plant eater?" (plant eater)

This lesson pairs with the Hadrosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Iguanodon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Iguanodon — one of the first dinosaurs science ever named — and teaches its action: reach out, strip the branch, munch, thumbs-up.

What is this?

Iguanodon was a plant eater that could walk on four legs or run on two, with a sharp beak, grinding teeth and one spike on each thumb.

What does it mean?

The iguanodon carries the deck’s best mistake-story: early scientists glued its thumb spike on its nose. Getting things wrong and fixing them IS science.

What does the child need to know?

Room for a reach and a munch. Hands do all the work — one arm reaches, one hand strips, the mouth munches.

Why this matters

Children learn that science corrects itself — the nose-horn mistake is funny, fixable and famous. The thumbs-up finish makes the spike unforgettable.

What it teaches

Two-hand coordination (reach and strip), the munch sequence, and story memory: where the spike went first, where it belongs now.

Words to learn

Iguanodonthumbspikemunchbeakmistakescience

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Iguanodon — one of the very first dinosaurs people ever found! Reach out... strip the branch... MUNCH, munch, munch! And here is its secret weapon — a spike on its THUMB! Thumbs up, iguanodon style!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: light green, standing on hind legs, one hand reaching forward.
  2. Tell the age: one of the FIRST dinosaurs ever named — people have known it for nearly two hundred years.
  3. Tell the mistake: early scientists thought the thumb spike was a nose horn! It took years to fix.
  4. Practice the action: reach one arm out, strip the pretend branch with the other hand, MUNCH with big chews.
  5. Finish with the spike: a big thumbs-up — the iguanodon signature.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a light-green iguanodon stands on its hind legs reaching forward with one hand — the reach-munch pose, spike ready on the thumb.

Ask your child

"Where does the spike really grow?" (on the thumb) "Where did scientists FIRST think it grew?" (on the nose — a famous mistake) "Show me the reach-and-munch."

What your child can say or do

Your child may end every meal with an iguanodon thumbs-up, correct the nose-horn story for the whole family, or reach-strip-munch every imaginary branch in the park.

Out in the real world

Science still corrects itself — that is its power. The thumb spike probably worked for hooking branches and for self-defense: a multitool, not a weapon first.

Try it together

Munch chains: reach, strip, munch, thumbs-up — repeat with branches at three heights. Harder: walk on four legs (hands and feet) between branches. Softer: seated reach-munch.

Understanding check

Ask: "Thumb spike or nose horn?" (thumb — the nose was the mistake) "Show me the munch." "Four legs or two?" (both — it could switch!)

This lesson pairs with the Iguanodon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Maiasaura — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Maiasaura, the deck’s parent, and teaches its action: cuddle, feed, tuck and pat — the full nest-care routine, swapped both ways.

What is this?

Maiasaura was a duck-billed plant eater that nested in big colonies and raised its babies there — feeding them until they grew strong.

What does it mean?

Care-taking play is empathy practice with a script: wrap, feed, tuck, pat. The swap round (being cared for) is the part children ask for again.

What does the child need to know?

One stuffed animal or doll as the baby dino. A cushion nest. Nothing else — the routine is the equipment.

Why this matters

Before this fossil, many people pictured dinosaurs as cold egg-abandoners. The maiasaura nests changed that forever — care IS dinosaur behavior.

What it teaches

Gentle-hand control (patting softly is a skill), routine memory (four steps in order), and role-swapping — caring and being cared for.

Words to learn

Maiasauranestbabymothergentlecolonycare

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Maiasaura — the good mother! She built a nest, laid her eggs, and brought food to her babies. Cuddle your baby dino... feed it leaves... tuck it in... pat, pat, pat. Now YOU be the baby — it is your turn to be cared for!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: mint-green, soft duck bill, gentle eye.
  2. Say its name meaning: good mother lizard — given because of what the fossils showed.
  3. Tell the nest fact: about thirty eggs in one nest, and parents brought food to babies IN the nest.
  4. Practice the action: cuddle the baby dino, pretend-feed it leaves, tuck it in the cushion nest, pat its head five times.
  5. Swap: now your child is the baby — be cared for, then swap back.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a mint-green maiasaura with a soft duck bill and gentle eye stands calmly — the good mother of the deck.

Ask your child

"What does maiasaura mean?" (good mother lizard) "How many steps in the nest routine?" (cuddle, feed, tuck, pat) "Who brings the food?" (the parents — for weeks)

What your child can say or do

Your child may nest every stuffed animal in the house, enforce pat-counts on siblings, or ask to be the baby one more time — the swap is the point.

Out in the real world

Penguins, wolves and most birds feed their babies the maiasaura way. Care is old, old behavior — the fossils proved dinosaurs joined the parenting club long ago.

Try it together

Nest rounds: full routine, then swap, then back. Harder: add a nest-check walk — pat, circle, pat. Softer: two steps — cuddle and pat — for the youngest caregivers.

Understanding check

Ask: "What did the fossils prove?" (dinosaurs cared for their babies) "Show me the four-step routine." "How many eggs in a nest?" (about thirty)

This lesson pairs with the Maiasaura flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Microraptor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Microraptor, the four-winged wonder, and teaches its action: flap all four wings fast, hold the spread glide, land on the next tree.

What is this?

Microraptor was a pigeon-sized gliding dinosaur with feathers on its arms AND its legs — four wings — and glossy black-blue feathers like a starling.

What does it mean?

Four-wing flapping is a body-awareness bonanza: hands AND feet working as wings, then holding a spread pose — control in a brand-new shape.

What does the child need to know?

Cushions as trees, floor as forest. The glide pose (arms and legs spread) needs a soft landing zone.

Why this matters

The microraptor proves flight was invented more than once and in more than one way — four wings is a whole different blueprint, and it worked.

What it teaches

Arm-leg coordination (four limbs, one job), spread-pose stillness, and the color fact: scientists can even know a dinosaur’s shine.

Words to learn

Microraptorfour wingsglidefeathersglossytreesspread

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Microraptor — four wings on one little body! Wings on the arms, wings on the legs! Flap, flap, flap them fast... hold your glide... land on the next tree! Shiny feathers, quick glides — the prettiest flyer in the forest!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: pink-magenta, wings on arms and legs, long feathered tail.
  2. Count the wings: one, two, three, FOUR — arms and legs both carry feathers.
  3. Tell the shine fact: fossil feathers kept their color — shiny black with blue-green sheen, like a starling.
  4. Practice the action: flap hands and feet fast for three seconds... hold the spread glide... land on a cushion tree.
  5. Tree-hop: glide cushion to cushion without touching the forest floor.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a pink-magenta microraptor glides with all four wings spread and a long feathered tail streaming behind — the tree-to-tree traveler.

Ask your child

"How many wings?" (four) "Where do the extra wings grow?" (on the legs) "What color were its feathers?" (shiny black-blue, like a starling)

What your child can say or do

Your child may spread-glide from cushion to cushion for days, inspect starlings for family shine, or count wings on every bird with new suspicion.

Out in the real world

Flying squirrels and gliding geckos still travel tree to tree without true flight — the microraptor’s plan, still working in today’s forests.

Try it together

Forest course: three cushion trees, four-wing flap before each glide. Harder: five-second spread holds. Softer: arm-wings only, feet on the floor.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me four wings." (hands and feet spread) "Bigger than or smaller than a pigeon?" (about the same) "What did its glide do?" (carried it between trees)

This lesson pairs with the Microraptor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Mosasaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Mosasaurus, the sea king, and teaches its action: one big swim stroke, a deep dive, then the jaw snap — the full hunt, three parts.

What is this?

Mosasaurus was a giant swimming reptile — not a dinosaur — with long toothy jaws, four flippers and a shark-style tail, breathing air at the surface.

What does it mean?

The mosasaurus sorts a big idea: dinosaur is a land word; the ancient seas belonged to reptile cousins. Same age, different address.

What does the child need to know?

Floor becomes ocean. Tummy for the swim stroke, arms for the sweep, hands for the snap. Nothing else required.

Why this matters

Every dinosaur-loving child eventually asks about the sea monsters — this card answers with the facts, and the whale comparison (air-breathing!) is the twist.

What it teaches

Big-arm coordination, the breath fact played as surfacing (up for air!), and the not-a-dinosaur distinction that sorts the whole ancient world.

Words to learn

Mosasaurusseaflippersjawssurfaceairreptile

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Mosasaurus — the king of the ancient sea! Long jaws, four flippers, a tail like a shark. Big swimming stroke... dive DOWN deep... pop up for air — it breathes like a whale!... and SNAP goes lunch!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: dark blue, long open jaws, four flippers, shark tail.
  2. Say the sort: not a dinosaur — a swimming reptile cousin, king of the same ancient seas.
  3. Tell the breath fact: it surfaced for air like a whale — no gills, lungs only.
  4. Practice the action: lie on your tummy... one BIG swimming stroke with both arms... dive down deep... pop up... SNAP those long jaws.
  5. Patrol: swim-stroke around the whole ocean floor, surfacing every few strokes for air.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a dark-blue mosasaurus swims with long jaws open, flippers spread and a shark-like tail — the sea king, mid-patrol.

Ask your child

"Dinosaur or sea reptile?" (sea reptile — a cousin) "How does it breathe?" (air at the surface, like a whale) "Show me the three-part hunt." (stroke, dive, snap)

What your child can say or do

Your child may declare bathwater Cretaceous, patrol the carpet in swim-strokes, or correct every "sea dinosaur" they meet — actually, a sea reptile.

Out in the real world

Whales prove the mosasaurus plan still works: air-breathing giants that rule the sea. Its living cousins are snakes and lizards — the monitor lizard is family.

Try it together

Ocean patrol: stroke across the room, surface twice, three snaps. Harder: snap only underwater-pretend (silent snaps). Softer: strokes from sitting, then lying down.

Understanding check

Ask: "Land or sea?" (sea) "Show me the surface-for-air pop." "What hunts with those jaws?" (fish, sharks — even other mosasaurs)

This lesson pairs with the Mosasaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Ouranosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Ouranosaurus, the sail-back plant eater, and teaches its action: arch up, grow the sail bigger, then flop flat and start again.

What is this?

Ouranosaurus was a plant eater with a tall rounded sail along its back, a duck-style bill and strong hind legs — a desert-edge browser.

What does it mean?

Growing a sail bigger and bigger is progressive effort made visible: small, bigger, BIGGEST — then the flop. Children read the scale in their own spine.

What does the child need to know?

Floor space to arch and flop. The game is safest on a soft rug with the flop ending every round.

Why this matters

The sail pairs with spinosaurus’s — same idea on two very different animals — and the warming-cooling explanation turns a shape into a tool.

What it teaches

Back and core control (the arch is real work), progressive size language (bigger, biggest), and the flop as a body reset.

Words to learn

Ouranosaurussailbackarchsunwarmbrave

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Ouranosaurus — the brave lizard with a sail! Arch your back... make your sail small... bigger... BIGGEST! Feel it catch the sun! Now flop — a tired dinosaur — and grow it one more time!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: teal, tall rounded sail along the back.
  2. Say the name meaning: brave lizard — it lived at the desert’s green edge.
  3. Tell the tool fact: the sail may have warmed it in morning sun and cooled it in shade — a built-in thermostat.
  4. Practice the action: arch your back, stretch arms back as the sail — small sail... bigger... BIGGEST.
  5. Flop flat like a tired dinosaur, then grow the sail again.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a teal ouranosaurus stands with a tall rounded sail along its back — the thermostat, worn on the outside.

Ask your child

"What grows along its back?" (a tall sail) "Show me small, bigger, biggest." "What might the sail do in the sun?" (warm it — and cool it in the shade)

What your child can say or do

Your child may arch-sail at every sunbeam, explain thermostats to the household, or flop-flat on request — the reset is half the fun.

Out in the real world

Sails are rare and wonderful: the dimetrodon carried one long before, and chameleons wear small ones now. Body parts that manage temperature are everywhere — ears, sails, big feet.

Try it together

Sail rounds: three grows and flops. Harder: hold biggest for five seconds. Softer: arms-on-floor version for early archers.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me your biggest sail." "What does the sail do?" (warms and cools the body) "Brave lizard or scared lizard?" (brave — it is the name)

This lesson pairs with the Ouranosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Oviraptor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Oviraptor — the deck’s great name-fix — and teaches its action: arms around the egg, slow guardian circles, no letting go.

What is this?

Oviraptor was a beaked, crest-headed dinosaur with a fluffy feathered tail, a strong beak for seeds and shellfish — and a fossil-proven habit of sitting protectively on its own nest.

What does it mean?

The oviraptor teaches fair judgment: it was named "egg thief" on thin evidence, and the fossils later cleared its name. Names are guesses until the facts come in.

What does the child need to know?

One ball or balled sock as the egg. Room for slow guardian circles around a cushion nest.

Why this matters

Every child meets unfair labels; the oviraptor is the dinosaur version — accused, cleared, vindicated by better evidence. Justice, paleontology edition.

What it teaches

Gentle holding under challenge (the egg stays safe even when someone reaches), slow-walking control, and evidence-based thinking in miniature.

Words to learn

Oviraptoreggnestguardnamemistakeevidence

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Oviraptor — the dinosaur with the unfair name! People called it an egg THIEF — but the fossils showed it was guarding its OWN babies! Cup your egg... wrap your arms around... slow guardian circles. Shhh — the babies are sleeping!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: light purple, curved head crest, fluffy tail.
  2. Tell the name trouble: "oviraptor" means egg THIEF — a name it got from being found near eggs.
  3. Tell the fix: one famous fossil shows it sitting ON its own nest, wings spread over its eggs — a parent, not a thief.
  4. Practice the action: cup your hands as the egg... wrap both arms around it... walk slow guardian circles.
  5. The challenge round: someone gently reaches for the egg — the guardian shields it without squeezing.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a light-purple oviraptor stands with a curved head crest and a fluffy feathered tail — the nest keeper, cleared by the evidence.

Ask your child

"What does its name mean?" (egg thief — but it is not true!) "What did the famous fossil show?" (it sitting on its own nest) "Show me the guardian circles."

What your child can say or do

Your child may guard cushions ferociously and gently at once, rename the oviraptor something fairer, or announce that scientists can be wrong — and then fix it.

Out in the real world
