Scientists still rename animals when evidence improves — the oviraptor is the famous case. Guarding behavior is everywhere today: robins dive at cats, penguins shuffle eggs onto their feet.

Try it together

Guard rounds: three slow circles, then a gentle steal attempt. Harder: two eggs, two arms, one guardian. Softer: guard while sitting, circles later.

Understanding check

Ask: "Egg thief or nest guardian?" (guardian — the name was unfair) "Show me the safe hold." "What proof cleared its name?" (a fossil sitting on its own nest)

This lesson pairs with the Oviraptor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Pachycephalosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Pachycephalosaurus, the dome-head, and teaches its action: pat the dome, stand on one leg, boop gently — softest bump takes the crown.

What is this?

Pachycephalosaurus was a plant eater with a dome of solid bone on its head — up to ten inches thick — and a bumpy back fringed with little knobs.

What does it mean?

Gentle-vs-hard is the whole game: a body built for bumping that still chooses soft contact. Manners, practiced by the best-helmeted dinosaur.

What does the child need to know?

A partner for the boop and floor space for one-leg standing. Walls within reach for wobbles.

Why this matters

Children hear "bone head" and expect crashes; the lesson lands the surprise — probably gentle shoves, not head-on hits. The softest-bump-wins rule makes it playable.

What it teaches

One-leg balance, pressure control (boop is a real skill), and turn-taking under excitement.

Words to learn

Pachycephalosaurusdomehelmetbumpgentleboopboss

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Pachycephalosaurus — the bone-dome dinosaur! A helmet as thick as ten fingers! Pat, pat your dome... stand on one leg... lean in... gentle BOOP! The softest bump is the boss!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: yellow, thick dome head, bumpy back.
  2. Say the thickness: the dome was solid bone, as thick as a stack of ten fingers.
  3. Tell the manner fact: head-to-head crashes would hurt BOTH dinosaurs — scientists think they leaned and shoved gently instead.
  4. Practice the action: pat your dome twice... stand on one leg... lean in for a gentle shoulder BOOP.
  5. Crown the round: the softest boop of the day is boss pachycephalosaurus.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a yellow pachycephalosaurus stands with a thick domed head and a bumpy back — the helmet, worn for gentle business.

Ask your child

"How thick was the dome?" (ten fingers of bone) "Hard bumps or gentle bumps?" (gentle — that is the game) "Show me the one-leg boop."

What your child can say or do

Your child may boop foreheads into every greeting, award boss crowns at random, or pat their own head twice before entering rooms — dome check.

Out in the real world

Bighorn rams and bison still settle rank with leaning shoves and hornclang — the gentle version, exactly. The dome was a crown first, a helmet second.

Try it together

Boop brackets: two at a time, softest boop advances. Harder: boop while both stand on one leg. Softer: boop a cushion between partners.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is on its head?" (a thick bone dome) "Show me the gentle boop." "Who wins the round?" (the softest bumper)

This lesson pairs with the Pachycephalosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Parasaurolophus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Parasaurolophus, the deck’s foghorn, and teaches its action: forearm crest up, one deep honk — then the herd’s answer.

What is this?

Parasaurolophus was a duck-billed plant eater with a long tube crest curving back from its skull — hollow, connected to its nose, able to boom deep calls.

What does it mean?

The parasaurolophus turns sound into distance: a call made to reach the FAR side of the valley. Loud-then-soft honks practice both ends of the volume dial.

What does the child need to know?

Voices and one forearm as the crest. Real deep honks come from the belly, not the throat — the practice finds them.

Why this matters

Scientists built a model of the crest’s tubes and PLAYED its sound — a real foghorn note you can look up. A dinosaur voice you can actually hear: unbeatable.

What it teaches

Breath depth (belly breaths for deep honks), volume control, and the model-making idea: science can reconstruct a sound.

Words to learn

Parasaurolophuscresttubehonkdeepvalleyherd

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Parasaurolophus — the foghorn dinosaur! A long tube crest on its head, and a call that crossed whole valleys! Forearm crest up... breathe deep from your belly... HOOOOONK! Now the herd answers — and then the whisper-honks!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: teal, long tube crest sweeping back.
  2. Trace the tube: out the back of the head, longer than the skull itself.
  3. Tell the played-sound fact: scientists made a model of the tubes and played a deep foghorn honk — the real dinosaur voice, rebuilt.
  4. Practice the action: rest a forearm along the back of your head as the crest... belly breath... one deep HOOOONK.
  5. Herd answers: everyone echoes — first loud, then the whisper-honk round for evening.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a teal parasaurolophus stands with a long tube crest curving back from its head — the foghorn, aimed at the far valley.

Ask your child

"Where does the crest point?" (backward, behind the head) "Show me the deep honk." "What did scientists build to hear it?" (a model of the crest’s tubes)

What your child can say or do

Your child may honk from the belly on demand — genuinely impressive depth — answer doors in foghorn, or demand the real recorded sound on repeat.

Out in the real world

Foghorns, tubas and conch shells all push air through long tubes — the crest’s design, still standard equipment. Deep calls carry farther: that is the valley trick.

Try it together

Call codes: one honk means gather, two means look, three means snack time. Harder: honk-matching — echo the exact volume. Softer: mouth-tube honks only.

Understanding check

Ask: "Tube crest forward or backward?" (backward) "Show me the belly breath." "What did scientists play?" (the real deep honk, rebuilt from the tubes)

This lesson pairs with the Parasaurolophus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Plateosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Plateosaurus, the deck’s pioneer, and teaches its action: pick three pretend leaves at three heights, then graze low on four legs.

What is this?

Plateosaurus was an early long-necked plant eater from before the giant sauropods, walking on four legs and rearing up on two to reach high branches.

What does it mean?

Switching feeding styles — reach high on two legs, graze low on four — is a body-plan lesson: one animal, two postures, chosen as needed.

What does the child need to know?

Room for three picking heights and a low graze. Hands as the reaching arm; the floor as the low meadow.

Why this matters

The plateosaurus is the deck’s history card for long necks: before brachiosaurus, before diplodocus, this pioneer worked out the reaching plan first.

What it teaches

Posture switching (two legs to four), height sorting (knee, shoulder, tiptoe), and the time-depth idea: 210 million years ago.

Words to learn

Plateosaurusreachlong neckfour legstwo legsearlyleaves

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Plateosaurus — one of the very first long necks! Stand up on two legs... reach the knee leaf... munch munch... the shoulder leaf... the tiptoe leaf! Now down on four legs — graze the meadow, low and slow."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: golden, long neck, upright, one arm out.
  2. Say its age: one of the FIRST long-necked plant eaters — 210 million years ago, long before T. rex.
  3. Tell the switch fact: it walked on four legs but reared up on two to reach high.
  4. Practice the action: pick a leaf at knee height (munch twice), shoulder height, tiptoe height.
  5. Graze round: down on four limbs, grazing the floor meadow like a four-legged dinosaur.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a golden plateosaurus stands upright on its hind legs with a long neck and one arm reaching out — the pioneer, mid-pick.

Ask your child

"Show me the two-leg reach." "Show me the four-leg graze." "Which came first — plateosaurus or brachiosaurus?" (plateosaurus — the pioneer)

What your child can say or do

Your child may rear-reach at every high shelf (supervised!), graze-crawl across rugs at bedtime, or announce 210 million years as their new favorite number.

Out in the real world

Bears do the switch today — four legs for walking, rearing up when the high fruit calls. The plateosaurus worked out the trick 210 million years early.

Try it together

Leaf rounds: three picks, three munches, one graze — full cycle. Harder: add a fourth leaf — jump-pick. Softer: seated picks, graze as a stretch.

Understanding check

Ask: "Two legs or four?" (both — it switched) "Show me the tallest pick." "Hunter or plant eater?" (plant eater — the first of the long-neck crowd)

This lesson pairs with the Plateosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Quetzalcoatlus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Quetzalcoatlus, the deck’s sky giant, and teaches its action: three enormous slow flaps, then a five-second glide, then the proud walk.

What is this?

Quetzalcoatlus was the largest flying animal ever found — a pterosaur standing as tall as a giraffe, with wings stretching about ten meters, stalking on the ground between flights.

What does it mean?

Slow is the giant’s speed: big slow flaps and long glides teach pace control — the opposite of the raptor’s quick steps, and just as hard.

What does the child need to know?

A long runway and arms that hold wide. The proud walk (tall, straight legs) is the ground half of the animal.

Why this matters

Size records fascinate children, and this one holds: no bigger flyer has ever been found. The giraffe-standing fact lands the scale before the wings even open.

What it teaches

Pace control (slow flaps on purpose), glide endurance (five full seconds), and tall-posture walking — the ground game.

Words to learn

Quetzalcoatlusgiantpterosaurwingspanglidestalkproud

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Quetzalcoatlus — the biggest flyer EVER! As tall as a giraffe, wings as wide as a plane! Big SLOW flaps... hold the glide... five whole seconds... land tall and walk proud. Giants never hurry!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: violet, huge wings, very long straight beak.
  2. Say the size: standing on the ground, as tall as a giraffe; wings out, as wide as a small plane.
  3. Tell the ground fact: it did not just fly — it STALKED on folded wings, walking proud and picking up meals.
  4. Practice the action: three enormous SLOW flaps... arms wide, glide for five seconds... land tall and walk proudly.
  5. Repeat — the giant never hurries.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a violet quetzalcoatlus flies with huge spread wings and a very long straight beak — the sky giant, unhurried.

Ask your child

"Taller than you or shorter?" (taller — giraffe height!) "Show me the slow flaps." "What does it do on the ground?" (stalks and walks, wings folded)

What your child can say or do

Your child may adopt the proud walk permanently, glide five-count across every rug, or inform the family that the biggest flyer ever is on the cards.

Out in the real world

Condors and albatrosses glide the quetzalcoatlus way — huge wings, few flaps, hours aloft. Watching an albatross is watching this lesson, live.

Try it together

Giant circuits: slow flaps, five-glide, proud walk — three circuits. Harder: seven-second glides. Softer: three-second glides with a lap to land on.

Understanding check

Ask: "Biggest flyer ever?" (yes — still the record) "Show me the proud walk." "Flap fast or slow?" (slow — giants never hurry)

This lesson pairs with the Quetzalcoatlus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Spinosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Spinosaurus, the river giant, and teaches its action as a three-part routine: arms up as the sail, swim-stroke low, then the snout snap.

What is this?

Spinosaurus was possibly the longest meat-eating dinosaur — with a tall back sail of spines, a long crocodile-style snout and a body built for fishing rivers.

What does it mean?

Three-part routines build sequence memory: sail, swim, snap. The spinosaurus also stretches the hunter idea — this giant hunted fish, patiently, in rivers.

What does the child need to know?

Room for the full routine. The sail is arms, the swim is shoulders, the snap is hands — one child, three jobs.

Why this matters

The sail pairs with ouranosaurus’s, the fishing pairs with baryonyx’s — and both pairings teach that shapes and habits repeat across the dinosaur world.

What it teaches

Sequencing (three parts in order), shoulder-arm control for the sweep, and the river-habitat idea — not every hunter chased on land.

Words to learn

Spinosaurussailspinessnoutriverfishroutine

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Spinosaurus — the river giant! A sail as big as a door on its back, a snout like a crocodile! Arms up — SAIL! Swim low... and SNAP, snap, snap those fish! Sail, swim, snap — the river giant’s dance!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: pink-magenta, tall sail, long snout.
  2. Say the record: possibly the LONGEST meat eater ever — longer than T. rex, some scientists think.
  3. Tell the spine fact: the sail’s spines grew taller than your whole arm, straight from its back.
  4. Practice the action: sweep both arms up behind your head — one big SAIL... then swim-stroke low... then snap the snout-hands three times.
  5. Run the routine: sail, swim, snap — again, in order, like a river dance.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a pink-magenta spinosaurus stands with a tall sail along its back and a long crocodile snout — the river fisher, routine ready.

Ask your child

"Show me the three parts." (sail, swim, snap) "What does it mostly eat?" (fish) "Whose sail is bigger — spinosaurus or ouranosaurus?" (spinosaurus — the spines are arm-tall)

What your child can say or do

Your child may run the routine at every bath, hook the sail pose into dance moves, or rank river fish by spino-snack size.

Out in the real world

Herons and gharials fish the spinosaurus way — patience, snout, strike. Recent fossils even showed paddle-style tail bones: the river giant grows more river-born every year.

Try it together

River rounds: full routine, then reverse it — snap, swim, sail (harder than it sounds). Harder: sail holds for five seconds. Softer: two parts first, snap added last.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the sail." (arms up behind) "What is the routine order?" (sail, swim, snap) "Land hunter or river fisher?" (river fisher — mostly)

This lesson pairs with the Spinosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Styracosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Styracosaurus, the crowned one, and teaches its action: fan the spike-arms, one brave step, hold the pose — then shuffle as a herd.

What is this?

Styracosaurus was a horned plant eater with a big frill ringed by six long spikes and one strong horn on its nose — a walking crown.

What does it mean?

Bravery as a practiced pose: step forward, hold still, stand tall. The herd shuffle adds the group rule — brave together, gentle together.

What does the child need to know?

Room for one brave step and a slow herd line. Fingers fan out as the spikes.

Why this matters

The styracosaurus is the deck’s bravest LOOK, and the lesson splits looking from doing: the crown says brave, the body walks gently. Appearances, examined.

What it teaches

Held-pose stillness (three counts), forward-step courage in a safe frame, and group-line control — the shuffle stays slow.

Words to learn

Styracosaurusspikescrownfrillbraveposeherd

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Styracosaurus — the crowned dinosaur! Six spikes around its frill, like a king’s crown! Fan your spikes... one brave step... hold it — one, two, three! Now the herd shuffles — brave and gentle, no bumping!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: orange, big frill ringed with spikes, one nose horn.
  2. Count the crown: six spikes ringing the frill — some as long as your arm.
  3. Say the honest part: the crown is for SHOWING — most days, the herd just eats and walks.
  4. Practice the action: fan your spike-fingers around your head... one brave step forward... hold the pose for three counts.
  5. Herd shuffle: line up, poses up, slow shuffle sideways — nobody bumps.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange styracosaurus stands with a big frill ringed in long spikes and one nose horn — the crown, worn walking-tall.

Ask your child

"How many frill spikes?" (six) "Show me the brave pose." (step, then hold for three) "What is the herd rule?" (brave together, gentle together — no bumping)

What your child can say or do

Your child may hold brave poses at doorways, crown every stuffed animal in spikes, or lead family shuffles with arm-fans up.

Out in the real world

Lion manes, peacock tails, elk antlers — the crown principle runs through nature: look magnificent first, use the hardware only if needed. The styracosaurus wore the best crown of all.

Try it together

Brave rounds: three step-and-holds, then a full herd shuffle. Harder: pose on one leg. Softer: seated pose with spike-fans only.

Understanding check

Ask: "What rings the frill?" (six long spikes) "Show me the brave step." "Spikes for showing or for bumping?" (for showing — gentle is the rule)

This lesson pairs with the Styracosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.

DINOSAURS LESSON · DINOSAURS · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Therizinosaurus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the Therizinosaurus, the claw record-holder, and teaches its action: wave the long claws slowly, then hook a high branch down for breakfast.

What is this?

Therizinosaurus was a tall plant eater with a small head, a round feathered body and the longest claws of any animal ever found — about half a meter each.

What does it mean?

The therizinosaurus splits looks from diet once and for all: the scariest claws in the fossil record belong to a leaf eater. Tools are not tempers.

What does the child need to know?

Room for wide claw-waves. An invisible high branch works; a real doorway frame marks the hook height perfectly.

Why this matters

The record itself is the hook: half-meter claws, verified by fossils. And the twist — gentle giant — is the deck’s kindest surprise.

What it teaches

Slow wide-arm control (the wave is feather-duster gentle), the hook-and-pull two-step, and the record book: longest claws EVER.

Words to learn

Therizinosaurusclawsrecordhookbranchgentleleaves

Say this to your child

“"Meet the Therizinosaurus — the claw champion! Claws longer than your whole ARM — the longest ever found! Wave them slowly... so long, so wavy! Now hook the high branch... pull it down... munch, munch. The giant claws pick the salad!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: pink-magenta, small head, round belly, three long claws per hand.
  2. Say the record: each claw about half a meter — the longest claws of ANY animal, ever found.
  3. Tell the twist: it ate LEAVES. The claws hooked branches down — dinner tools, not fighting tools.
  4. Practice the action: arms wide, fingers long — wave the claws slowly, like feather dusters.
  5. Breakfast: hook the high branch... pull it down... munch the leaves. The monster claws serve the salad bar.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a pink-magenta therizinosaurus stands with a small head, round belly and three very long claws showing on each hand — the champion, mid-wave.

Ask your child

"How long were the claws?" (about half a meter — longest ever) "Meat eater or plant eater?" (plant eater!) "Show me the feather-duster wave."

What your child can say or do

Your child may duster-wave at every high shelf, hook imaginary branches for the whole family’s salad, or declare the therizinosaurus their favorite record-holder.

Out in the real world

Sloths hook branches with long curved claws today — same plan, slower living. And the record stands: no claw, horn or tusk in the fossil book beats the therizinosaurus.

Try it together

Breakfast rounds: wave, hook, pull, munch — at two branch heights. Harder: three branches before the munch. Softer: seated waves, one hook to finish.

Understanding check

Ask: "Whose claws were the longest ever?" (therizinosaurus) "Show me the hook and pull." "What did the giant claws do?" (hooked branches down for leaves)

This lesson pairs with the Therizinosaurus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Dinosaurs.
